utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to ask you something else about this, please. Can you look at the column where the identification number is and the number that is supposed to be your identification number. Please look at that number, the identification number column, and look the your number, and here it says 0104964. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree then that that is your date of birth? It is actually not or neither can it be your identification number? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the date of my birth, not my identification number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you agree also that for it to be your date of birth there must be a 1 between the 4 and the 9? Just look at the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. For it to be complete it should be the 1st of April, 1964.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in this number the 1 of 19 is missing. I guess the point Madam Vidovic is making.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Your Honours, what I'm trying to clarify here is this:

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However it is, Mr. Ajman, this is not your ID number.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It is not, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the data that refer to you in this list is not accurate?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only correct thing is the first and the last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can put this document away now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Is it possible that an identification number was given corresponding to the date of birth of a member of the army, especially if they were foreigners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how they made up these numbers, how the numbers were formed. Most probably they took the Bosnian number, the way the Bosnians have identification numbers. In our countries we don't have these ID numbers. Maybe this is a new thing. Maybe they took the first part of that, and since there is no second part of the ID number, maybe they just added that. I mean this is just my take on it. Perhaps it was done in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't know whether that was your ID number or not, or are you aware of another identification number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have any other number. First name, last name, that's it. All that is here is all that there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In relation to what I said, and in fairness to you, Mr. Awad, I just want to comment that I note that the numbers on that column, which look like they could be date of birth, all miss the 1 of the 9 -- of the 1900 figure. All of them. Thank you. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, please, I have not understood the purpose of bringing this document. What -- what is it that you want to show, that --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to show that -- this is a document tendered by the Prosecutor, and I would like to show that the list does not contain reliable data, not as far as -- it doesn't contain reliable data and that it is not -- that it cannot be used as an exhibit or as evidence. If your permit me, I am going to clarify this very clearly with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, but -- but then in doing so, I ask you then to -- to explain to us the importance of -- of the information given in these documents. Even if they are unreliable, then what? What does that show? I mean, I accept your proposition that there are probably mistakes in these documents, but nevertheless, the witness is being listed as being a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment, and I guess that's all we need to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is information -- well, this is an exhibit tendered by the Prosecutor, and I believe that perhaps the name of the witness is what is relevant for the Court at this time. However, the Defence -- I have -- the Defence has its own view of the facts, and at this point in time it would be very complicated and we would lose a lot of time for me to go into that explanation, but I believe that the fact is very relevant -- or I believe it is very relevant to prove the fact that these lists are unreliable regardless of the fact that they contain the name of the witness, and I have several reasons for doing that. Your Honours, would you allow me to carry on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see Judge Harhoff nods his head in agreement, so you may carry on now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I cannot see because of the screen that is in front of Judge Harhoff, so I cannot actually see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct, and that's why I was -- I talked, and it is also necessary to place it on the record that your question is answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, from what I understood, you were given the citizenship of Bosnia and Herzegovina at one point in time. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You got it. Please, it's true, isn't it, that you were given a personal ID card, an ID document, in other words. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, do you remember that this document contained something that is an ID number?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did have this personal identification number. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't catch all the numbers, I'm afraid. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpret said she didn't catch all the numbers that Mr. Awad had mentioned. 0104964 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 010496190089.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did you get that identity document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1995. I -- maybe April. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: According to the law of '93 -- [Interpretation] according to the law -- law -- law of '93 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twenty-three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Twenty-three. So that was before the 26th of February, 19 -- oh, it is after 1996. Okay. You may proceed. Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of my question, Mr. Awad, was that in that list we do not see this personal ID number that you had already in 1995.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we can remove this document unless Your Honours have additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document may be removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could now Witness look at P2732, P2732.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, for the record I wish to say that this is a document of the 3rd Corps command, dated the 27th of October, 1995, and entitled "Instruction on the engagement and records to be kept of foreign citizens in the BH army." Would you please read points 3 and 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document stipulates that foreign citizens who are in the units from before, in the units of the BH army, as the document says, shall make a statement that they joined the army units voluntarily. It is true, isn't it, that members of the detachment did not make such statements about voluntarily joining the army up until the detachment was demobilised?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only did they not give such statements, they didn't wish to make such statements. They refused.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document be given an exhibit number, and I should like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 1138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, why did you not wish to state publicly that you had entered the ABiH voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Foreign volunteers felt that there was no need for any kind of documents, for any kind of acknowledgements or anything like that. They didn't wish to have any kind of official paper which would show that they had been fighters in the ABiH. They didn't wish to have any kind of document. They felt that this was unimportant for them and that it would detract from the value of their struggle. If I have come, I have come voluntarily, but I don't have to prove to anyone that I did so. I don't have to sign a paper saying that, so that there was no need. They considered that absolutely unimportant and unnecessary, and they didn't wish to make such statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But their voluntary participation in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was, nevertheless, the basis for applying for Bosnian citizenship. So why would anyone be reluctant to say that, "We have arrived here voluntarily and joined the fight," and on that basis apply for citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you that maybe 20 or 25 men, certainly not more than 30, acquired citizenship in this way that you have just described. He was given a certificate saying that he was a member of the BH army, and he submitted that document to the police, and they received citizenship. They were very few in number. And these people did provide their proper data in the list. Those who wished to, they did provide their proper data. Others did not, so they didn't. The other members did not apply for citizenship, nor did they need it. They didn't feel obliged to make any kind of statements, because they had absolutely no need for it. What is more, I think that Abu Mali or Sheik Anwar Shaaban, if he had told these people that they had to make such statements, they would have been told off, because they felt this to be an insult. "Why do I have to prove to anyone that I am a volunteer?" Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you file a declaration of voluntary admission to the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if you refuse to declare that you participated in the army on a voluntary basis, in that case were you recruited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please explain to me? Maybe I'm a woman and I know very little about military matters I need a little more explanation, so could you explain that to me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as recruitment or mobilisation is concerned, we were not citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so we could not come under the law of mobilisation. If we didn't -- if we had been members and didn't join, then we would be considered deserters, but our people came on a voluntary basis, without anybody's command or organisation. When they joined the El Mujahedin Detachment, they didn't need to prove that they were members. They didn't need any kind of document or any paperwork that they might use later on in life. It was sufficient for them to have come. For them that was sufficient proof that they are volunteers. Have you understood me? Why do I have to prove that I'm a volunteer? Maybe it's difficult for you to understand this, but that is how it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you didn't make this declaration, how did you get your citizenship under law 23?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I provided my data, and I did receive a certificate saying that I was a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this certificate was something that I received before the date of this document, because I applied in March or February, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Talking about citizenship, could I ask the technicians to play a video clip, VD18, of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, let me ask you, this person that you saw, a representative of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, said that a certain number of foreign citizens had forged documents on their participation in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whereas in fact they had not participated and on that basis they had obtained citizenship. According to what you know personally, were there such cases?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain this at the beginning. Regarding the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment who acquired citizenship on the basis of a certificate saying that they were members of the army, this was quite regular. There were cases that a certain number of students or people who were living in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and who were never members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, either for money or as a favour were given such certificates and did acquire citizenship. And unfortunately, as this date is completely deformed, their citizenship was confirmed, whereas those of us who acquired citizenship legally are being deprived of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ajman.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this video clip be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please give us the number of that video clip, madam, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] VD18, VD18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. VD18 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 1139, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see another video clip. It is a very brief one. Could the technical department play VD19 for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Awad, now that you have seen this video clip, is what you have said on this video correct? Is this what you have just been telling us?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to tender this video clip into evidence too. Let me just add and repeat that it is VD19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. VD19 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 1140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, let me ask you some more questions. Testifying yesterday, you mentioned on a number of occasions Arab humanitarian organisations, and you said also that you came to Bosnia-Herzegovina through one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like the witness to be shown D769. D769. For the record, it is a document of the security services centre in Zenica, 24th of November, 1995. It contains a list of foreign humanitarian organisations operating in the territory covered by the security services centre of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So will you please take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're struggling with our files here to get this number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Here it is. We have to go back in the file.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: These documents don't follow each other chronologically. They are not coming -- the way they are tendered into court, so we're having serious problems trying to follow you, Madam Vidovic. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm aware of that. How -- it's the fault of Mr. Mundis, because I have followed his sequence in the examination without really putting the documents in order. I know that I included in the binder far more documents than I had to. I hope you've now found D769.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I would like to ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have -- we have, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you see a list of humanitarian organisations, and all these were operating in the territory of Zenica. The one under number 4, Mowafaq foundation with its seat in Zenica, was that the humanitarian organisation that you mentioned having come through it to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it was -- that another humanitarian organisation was active, that is the Islamic Balkanic Centre [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Islamic Balkan Centre was a humanitarian organisation. It was a centre. Now, whether it acted as a humanitarian centre I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But was it operating in the territory of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about the High Saudi Committee? Was it also active in the territory of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about Igasa? Igasa, was it also active there?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How about Human Relief International?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is still active in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 1141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, let me ask you a question relating to Exhibit 1130. Exhibit 1130. If you remember, it was a document in which two members of the El Mujahid Detachment is mentioned, and one of them was Mr. Fazlic, and the other was Norudin [phoen] Alihodze. These were people who went to the school that is known as Ros, R-o-s, the officers' wartime school of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the wartime officers' school, R-o-s, or Ros.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think perhaps it is not necessary to show the witness the document as he remembers it well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you something in connection with it. Do you agree that both of these persons are local Bosnians, Muslims, locals?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not a single foreigner attended the Ros, did they?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me also ask you some questions regarding the operations at Vozuca, the Ozren-Vozuca pocket in July 1995 and in September 1995. I'll ask you, Mr. Awad, about the July operation first, which you described yesterday. Before the July operation you interpreted discussions about the evacuation and aid to be given to the wounded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, prior to the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that will the detachment at the time was formally resubordinated to the 35th Division; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would put it to you and ask for you to comment if I submit that General Sakib Mahmuljin was the commander of the 3rd Corps at the time of the preparations for the July operation, which you testified about yesterday, that he was in the area of Sarajevo working on the deblockade of Sarajevo. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that as far as I remember, there were no meetings with General Mahmuljin. So you have now reminded me that the deblocking of Sarajevo was underway at the time, so it is quite possible what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you're not at all sure that General Sakib Mahmuljin was in contact with the detachment during the preparations for the July operation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, you told us that the detachment called the operation Al Karame [phoen].

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Al Karame, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you knew that there was an exchange of 10 or 11 prisoners of war. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned a meeting after the Al Karame operation with representatives of the division at their request. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a meeting with them. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that at that meeting Abu Mali was present. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that meeting did Abu Mali mention any prisoners of war to Commander Hasanagic? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether that was discussed. I can't claim that. I can't be sure. I can't remember. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In any case, you knew that -- you knew of the existence of these prisoners of war after the July operation. Did you find out, see, or hear that any or all of these prisoners of war were mistreated by members of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither saw or heard anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you about the attitude of the El Mujahedin Detachment towards the prisoners of war. Have you ever heard of something called the Geneva Conventions on Prisoners of War?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is this convention that regulates the warfare and methods of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, did the El Mujahedin Detachment have their own rules relating to prisoners of war and, if yes, what were they?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't an official rule, as it were, but there was a general understanding that we should treat such prisoners humanely. I even saw a video clip showing people talking with the prisoners of war, giving them some biscuits and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, tell me this: You're a Muslim. You know the religious precepts. It is true, isn't it, that Islam as its own precepts relating to the treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are such precepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what they are?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they state that you have to treat them in a humane manner and that they have certain rights, that they should not be treated cruelly and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did the El Mujahedin Detachment abide by these precepts?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct, is it not, that the corps command, in fact, forwarded copies of the Geneva Convention to the detachment? Would you accept what I put to you?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything like that, that anything like that came to a detachment, was received there, and in view of the fact that this was a religious detachment, I'm not even sure that it would have been accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, did you have occasion to read this Convention? Does it differ, in effect, from what the Islamic precepts and attitudes toward prisoners of war are?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to read it before, earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, you cannot exclude the possibility that this convention was actually forwarded to the El Mujahedin Detachment? It's a whole separate issue whether it would have been accepted or not, but you cannot exclude the possibility that it was forwarded to the detachment?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is that possibility. I cannot claim either way. I did not have it in my hand, so I can't say either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We might as well just put one more question in this respect, because we're going to get there any way, and the question, of course, will be whether the rules that the witness has just told us about, the -- the internal -- if I may use this expression, the internal rules applying to prisoners of war would also apply to infidels.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we had no prisoners of war who were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question was: If the rules that would apply that the -- that the El Mujahid Detachment had developed or had brought with them relating to the treatment of prisoners of war, whether there would be any distinction as to how you would treat prisoners of war who were also Muslims or prisoners of war who were infidels or not Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are rules that apply to non-Muslims, because we never had Muslim prisoners of war. We were not in conflict with Muslims to have such prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me then put my question more directly. Would there have been different rules applying to a Muslim prisoner of war, or would, in your understanding the rules be the same regardless of whether the prisoner of war was a Muslim or a non-Muslim? Was there in any word -- in other words, any distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very broad question. So if we're talking about warfare between Muslims there are certain rules, and when the warfare -- when the war is waged against non-Muslims, the rules are different. But as far as prisoners of war are concerned, they are to be treated in a humane way. If you -- if you had a prisoner of war who was Muslim, you would not be allowed to take his booty, war booty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Suppose you would discover that come of the prisoners who were taken by the El Mujahid Detachment turned out to be Muslim, would he then be subjected to different treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot proceed from that proposition because that was not how it was nor would it be, because this detachment was not fighting Muslims, and whatever is non-existent I cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Suppose, just to take an example, a prisoner of war who had been taken by the El Mujahid Detachment would decide to change his religion and become a Muslim, would that then make him subject to different treatment? Just take it as an example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he would no longer be a prisoner of war. He would be a Muslim, which would mean that he would not be a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the detachment was there a procedure of interrogating war prisoners -- or prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were not in the least interested in having information about the enemy and the conduct of the conflict by the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say no, it means I don't know whether anybody interrogated them or not. I didn't have any contact with them. I didn't do any security work, so I really don't know whether anyone was interrogated or not. But certainly we needed information about their numerical strength, for instance. In any army that applies. But as far as I know -- or, rather, I don't know whether anyone interrogated those prisoners of war because I had no contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if they were interrogated, there would have been another interpreter instead of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who would question them. The detachment was of a mixed composition. There were Muslim -- there were foreigners, and there were Bosniak Muslims. So I don't know if anybody questioned them, but I did not have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there other people who spoke directly to the prisoners and who were not persons who only spoke Arabic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I could notice, the guards were Bosniaks, and I don't know if they talked with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, I will dwell very briefly on this topic. When you say "guards," "Bosniaks," you are referring to Bosniak members of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more thing. Tell us, you fought in this area against the army of Republika Srpska, and you said that you knew that there were some prisoners of war. These were people of Serbian ethnicity. In other words, not Muslim. They were Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, the rules that you mentioned a few moments ago, the precepts regulating the conduct and treatment of war -- prisoners of war that you said existed, which regulated that the treatment should be humane, those precepts would also apply to those prisoners of war, in other words, to those Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you a few questions about the Farz operation. This was an operation entitled Farz, and this name as assigned by the Bosnia-Herzegovina army; is that right? The detachment had their own name for this operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- this operation was called the Farz operation before the actual operation. It was determined by the army, and after the successful execution of this operation the detachment had a different name for it. They called it Bedr Al-Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bedr Al-Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bedr Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let me ask you this: During this operation, the Bedr Bosnia operation, or Farz, did you ever hear that members of the El Mujahedin Detachment took 61 prisoners of war, members of the Republika Srpska army, and took them to the thirteenth kilometre -- to the camp at the thirteenth kilometre?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you this: The camp was small. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a small area at the foot of a hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, would you agree with me 60 people, that's a large number of people? It's not just six people. It's a significant number of people.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This would mean that this could be three combat groups in terms of numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if so many people were taken prisoner -- prisoner of war and brought to this camp, the thirteenth kilometre camp, would you have heard about this?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. If I heard of imprisonment of ten people, of course I would have heard for a greater number of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you attended the meeting held on the 10th or 11th of September in 1995, and you said that General Sakib Mahmuljin also attended this meeting. In other words, the 3rd Corps commander. Tell me this: Did anyone make any mention on this occasion of the taking of 61 Serb prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please try to recollect another thing. You mentioned yesterday that as far as you could remember, this meeting was also attended by the commander of the 328th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he at any point in time during this meeting make any mention of his group having taken these prisoners of war, these 61 people, and that the -- that Mujahedin had seized these people?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did he in any manner complain of the conduct of members of the El Mujahedin Detachment in that respect?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this meeting. Not at this meeting, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Awad. I will have another question. You described -- you told us that you knew of a group of prisoners of war and that this group had been handed over. Was there any reason why the El Mujahedin Detachment would hand over a group of prisoners of war and kill off another group of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no logic to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have one last question, and I think this will complete my cross-examination. Mr. Awad, I would now just like to briefly touch upon the topic of commanding and the relationship between the detachment and the army. Let us take a hypothetical situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you getting on to the last topic before the end or the last question before the end? If it is the last topic, would this be a convenient time to take the break and you can start the topic later? But if it's the question, I'm prepared to stay here another two minutes for you to finish the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said last question, and I think it will not be long, the actual question, the last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, I would like to ask you just to imagine the following situation: Can you imagine that the president of the Presidency and the General Staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina ordered the replacement of the entire leadership of the El Mujahedin Detachment, thus Abu Mali, the military commander Muatez, the Sheik. Please, would this decision be accepted by the detachment or would it wait for the Shura's decision or act pursuant to the position that the Shura would take in that situation?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely it would not accept it. It would accept the Shura's decision. What the Shura decided, that's how it would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, and just one small question. These views of yours, were they also known to the people from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that you communicated with?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, they knew that we had our internal order. I don't know if they knew whether we would act like this. This is something else. Perhaps some did know and some did not and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a fair answer. Mr. Awad, I would like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will then take a break and come back at half past 1.00. Court adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has just a few final questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, on how many occasions did the El Mujahedin Detachment refuse to go where the ARBiH ordered the detachment to go?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I recall, this did not happen once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, on how many occasions did the El Mujahedin Detachment launch an attack on its own initiative without the ARBiH ordering such an attack?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to explain here. For any action, any attack would be preceded by agreement. When we agreed with the command of the corps or the division. Once an agreement was reached pursuant to a specific order or something. Nothing could happen without this agreement taking place. So this really needs to be explained properly. Therefore, the detachment never went anywhere on its own, but it would go for an agreement first. Once the agreement was reached or they were summoned, only then would they proceed to go off on an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us -- you spent -- you were asked a number of questions about the role of the Shura in the disbandment of the detachment, and my question to you, sir, is: In the absence of an order from the ARBiH to disband the detachment, in the absence of such an order, how likely would it have been for the Shura, on its own initiative, to make the decision to disband the detachment?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to speak logical things. Shura and the people in the detachment had come to fight, so how would they then just give up the fight themselves? If they wished to fight, there must be some kind of cause or reason for the Shura to make a decision to disband the unit and to stop fighting. Since pressure was exerted in Dayton on the Bosniak side to stop the war and to end the fighting, and this was the desire of the late President Alija Izetbegovic and the desire of these people here, then the Shura took into account this wish and the interest of the Bosniak people and adopted such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that part of your testimony. My question, though, is how likely would it have been for the Shura, on its own, to take the decision to disband the unit had there not been an order from the ARBiH to do so?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It most probably could have reached such a decision if there was no longer any need to fight or if it was not satisfied with the fighting in Bosnia. Then it could reach such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Awad?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no questions arising from the questions of the Prosecutor. I may have some questions arising from Your Honours' questions, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. I -- I made a boo-boo there. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in view of the fact that I speak in French and that I'm listening to you in English, will you please speak slowly in providing the answers so that I can understand you properly. Have you understood what I've asked? Thank you. I have several questions. You came to ex-Yugoslavia to study in 1982. When the war broke out you moved to Bosnia. On what basis did you make that decision, on an individual basis or by decision of your organisation or any other organisation or institution?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reached the decision myself on my own initiative, without anyone's organising -- organisation or suggestion. I made the decision when I saw what was happening to the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, listening to the stories of the refugees who came to Rijeka in Croatia. That's when I was working to receive all these refugees, and I was working on humanitarian tasks. And I decided that elderly people can also do those tasks, people who are older, and that I as an able-bodied young man can go to Bosnia and Herzegovina and contribute more. I can participate in something that was far greater. The main reason why I came was that I am a Muslim and of -- practising, practising Muslim, and I felt that it was my duty to help the Muslims who were suffering. This is why I made this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Did you have a sufficient amount of money, you personally, or did your humanitarian organisation provide you with the funds to come to Bosnia, to pay for your stay in a hotel and -- in a hotel, and later to rent an apartment?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I worked for a humanitarian organisation. I joined the organisation, the Mowafaq foundation, thinking that they were organising training for soldiers in Bosnia and Herzegovina, for Bosniak soldiers in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I wanted to work as an interpreter and translator, and I also wished to participate in the fighting. When I was asked by the director of the humanitarian organisation, the Mowafaq Foundation, who wanted to enter Bosnia or who wanted to go to Bosnia, to be there, and he said that there was a possibility for that, I used that option, and I entered Bosnia and Herzegovina at the expense of the humanitarian organisation that I was working for. Excuse me. I was receiving a salary at this organisation, so this is what I used to live on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now ask you to clarify something, if you can, in connection with the document that has been admitted into evidence, 1126, in which it says that the Arabs were sent by the Croats on a mission in support of the HVO. This document was signed, if I'm not mistaken, by the commander for morale of the 7th Muslim Brigade, Adilovic. Do you know anything about this, whether Arabs, and you yourself, perhaps, came because there was a mission by foreigners in support -- decided in support of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question properly, I see that perhaps this document was not translated to you properly, the document that you referred to. The document says that three Arabs were captured by the HVO. They did not go to assist the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps the document can be put on the ELMO so that we can all see it. That might be the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be very helpful, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the first paragraph of this document. If I'm not mistaken, there's reference to foreign citizens who are in our republic on benevolent missions, useful missions, by the Croatian Defence Council units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess -- I guess the translation of this document was done a little badly; correct? The translation should be: "We would like to hereby inform you -- inform the 3rd Corps about the foreign citizens who are in the republic on benevolent and useful missions who are captured by the Croatian Defence Council units." That's how it should have been. Now the verb has been put so far away from the noun that it causes the confusion that you are suffering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it is clear. [Interpretation] You told us during the examination-in-chief that you received a camouflage uniform from a member of the 7th Muslim Brigade, if I'm not mistaken, the commander for -- for morale, perhaps, Brzina, something like that. During the cross-examination, you told us, in response to a question put to you by Madam Vidovic, that this uniform was given to you by a military commander, to a humanitarian worker, because that is what you were at the time, in the form of a present. Was it normal for humanitarian workers to receive as gifts military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was normal at that time, and that's how I got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you know that that's a rule that humanitarian workers, in order to be able to work and during combat operations, they are supposed to assist the persons participating in combat, they had to have a sign, an emblem, something that will distinguish them. So did you have any such emblem or symbol to distinguish you from others?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any emblem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm talking of the period before you decided to become a combatant, a fighter, the first period of your stay here as a humanitarian worker, as you told us.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have an ID as a humanitarian worker. I didn't have any insignia. I didn't wear any insignia as a humanitarian worker. Yes, just slowly. I am going to explain everything. The Mowafaq Foundation, as a humanitarian organisation, was just in the process of being registered. It had just submitted its documents for registration to Croatia, in Zagreb, and the Foreign Ministry protocol, or whichever ministry dealt with the humanitarian organisations, in order to process documents, the admission of requests and the decision on the organisation, would usually take a month, two, or even three months, so that practically when I entered Bosnia and Herzegovina the Mowafaq Foundation had still not received any insignia or any documents that its workers could carry. I had joined the organisation. I was in Zagreb, and I was working for that organisation for only 15 days. Then I entered Bosnia and Herzegovina. Earlier I explained why I joined the organisation, and it was when I thought that they were actually organising this training in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I didn't have any insignia or any documents from that humanitarian organisation. As for the uniform, I received it on the day that I decided to be with the Mujahedin. Halil Brzina didn't know about this decision of mine. He knew me as a humanitarian worker. And I can say that this was a friendly, an ahbab [phoen] way that he gave me this uniform when I asked him for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two more small questions for you. This in particular that you just said, I didn't quite understand from your testimony how you decided to join the detachment precisely when it was decided to formally establish it.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what my wish was and what my objectives were when I came to Bosnia. On the day of the incident in Zenica and the humiliation that I experienced from the HVO police, and the humiliation that I experienced from the Bosnian police who were unable to protect me as a man. They were helpless. The HVO was insulting me, and the other guys were keeping quiet and just watching. No one was protecting me. And when I came to Bibista [as interpreted], I decided there will be no return, only fighting, fighting, and fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you already had relations with the commanders of the detachment, which still hadn't been formally established.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met those people before, for example, at markets, in mosques, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. My last question: The order to demobilise and to leave the country, was it given in a general fashion, or was it individually for each foreigner who was present on the territory of Bosnia and who had participated in the defence of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was a general one that applied to foreigners. The decision in Dayton referred to foreigners in general. It didn't name anyone in particular, that they had to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the Dayton Accords. But afterwards, the implementation of those accords or the provisions of the Dayton Accord, in those Bosnia legislation. Was it a general provision, or was it directed against each and every foreigner present here?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was a general decision. It was not directed at individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I would like to address a question to the parties, because I'm not quite sure if the witness's statement has been admitted into evidence. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, it is not. It's not been tendered by either party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Awad, you told us that the military academy at Ros at one point was anticipated to receive two persons from the El Mujahid Detachment to be trained as officers in the ABiH. And I think you also told us that these two persons actually never joined the school; is that correct? Sorry, let me just clarify.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They became officers. Not only did they join the school or enroll at the school, they also became officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. Now, how was the El Mujahid Detachment financed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly by donations from the Islamic world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if the ABiH supported the El Mujahid Detachment financially, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not financially. We had our own logistics, our own logistics, own service. Maybe in operations we would ask for some materiel and equipment, maybe some ammunition or certain types of weaponry that would not -- we did not have, or ammunition for the weapons if we didn't have it and we couldn't buy it, and then we would get something from the corps. Otherwise, we had our own independent logistics, and we were own stronger than the corps as far as that is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Logistics, what does that mean? Would that include armory, artillery?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything, generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you were able to purchase for -- the El Mujahedin itself was able to purchase artillery and to get it by independent means, that is to say not from the army? Is that correct, or how was it?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because we were buying weapons. The factory that was manufacturing weapons, Bratstvo of Novi Travnik, is where we bought a rocket launcher, and we also bought a 120-millimetre mortar. They were really not supposed to sell those things just like that, but we, nevertheless, did buy it from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And then I understand that you were also able, at some point at least in time, to seize weapons from the enemy.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To a great degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So let me return to the question. What sort of artillery were you given by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if any?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't get anything from the army, no weaponry at all, whether it was mortars or howitzers or any other weapons. No. No. We had 120-millimetre mortar, two 80-millimetre mortars. Then later in actions we captured a mountain gun. I think it was a ZIS recoilless gun. We captured a tank, a lot of ammunition, many rifles, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me just be clear about this. So what you are saying is that you received logistical support from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but you never received any weaponry, be it artillery or infantry weapons. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once we received about 100 rifles, I think, but those rifles were returned. When the detachment was disbanded, then the weaponry was also returned to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I was just going to come to that, because I think you told us earlier that all the weaponry that you had gathered was handed over to the 3rd Corps when the El Mujahid Detachment was disbanded, and that would include the rifles that you have just mentioned to us, the infantry -- light infantry weapons that you had been given by the ABiH, and all the weapons that you had purchased on your, and also the weapons that you had captured from the enemy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, I would be interested then to turn to the second and the third attack in 1995. In the July operation, you mentioned that you heard of some -- a group of some ten prisoners of war. You may have explained this already, but I would like you to repeat exactly what it was you heard about these ten prisoners of war. Do you know where they were taken and where they were held and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that they were held at a camp at the thirteenth kilometre, in a building. It was a hard building, not a tent. I saw a guard standing there outside, so I inferred from that that they were inside. These prisoners were handed over to the military police of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know why they were handed over?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was normal for them to be handed over to be exchanged. There was no need for us to keep them there and guard them, so they would be exchanged, whether it would be through the Red Cross or through the various exchange commissions. So they could be exchanged for Bosniaks or members of the army that had been captured. That is most probably what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if the ICRC, the Red Cross, was involved at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, while they were captured and held by the El Mujahedin Detachment the Red Cross was not involved. As for what happened later on, I don't know. I have no knowledge about the activities of the Red Cross or the -- or the 3rd Corps afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. I was just checking if the ICRC visited the Kamenica camp where they were held, but that was not the case, I understand.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were you staying at the Kamenica camp at that time? Were you living there?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the thirteenth kilometre, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where were you staying at that time?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- when the preparations were being done for the operation, I slept in the Brezik school or the village of Livade. Before that I stayed in Zenica. I had an office close to the commander. I was a kind of secretary there, so that I would be close to the commander to receive guests or somebody who wanted to talk to the commander. So I was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When did you see the guard outside the house where the prisoners were kept? Was that during a visit or -- or how come you -- I mean, you must have been present at the Kamenica camp when you saw the guard standing outside the house. So what were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who I came with, whether it was the commander or someone else. Anyway, he came there to inform the emir in the camp regarding future activities, to see whether new scouts, new groups should be engaged as the Arabs were staying there, and whether the operation needed to be continued, then scouts who were put up there needed to be used for that purpose. I can't remember exactly, but I did visit the camp, and I did see the guard. I saw the guard standing there in front of this building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you visit the Kamenica camp frequently at that time? Did you come there very often or ...

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so often. Not so often. I had no need to stay in that camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When did you -- or, rather, when you visited the Kamenica camp the next time were there still guards outside the house?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think so. After that I went to Zenica. I stayed for quite some time there before the preparations for the third operation. So I didn't go to the camp often. And the last time I went there there were no guards. They weren't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Who told you about the ten prisoners who had been held in Kamenica? How did you learn about there being prisoners kept there?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw two prisoners when the small Arab captured two of them, and the story was that there were prisoners there, which is quite normal. I heard that there was a certain number. I didn't know exactly how many until I saw the list which I signed when the military police took over those prisoners, because my signature is on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if any prisoner remained at Kamenica after the group had been transferred to the 3rd Corps in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one was left behind. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me then turn to the operation in September, the Farz operation. Although your statement has not been admitted into evidence, I think you mentioned somewhere in your statement that you saw three women being detained. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And -- and my question is: Where were you staying at the time in September 1995? Did you visit Kamenica, or did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: To go to the camp at the thirteenth kilometre, I would go there briefly. I was staying at the Brezik, and there was a school there where we were billeted, and that is where I slept, in Brezik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you remember if you visited Kamenica -- the thirteenth kilometre camp after the Farz operation?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't visit that camp again, as we continued towards Brizna [phoen], Maglaj. So neither the commander nor Muatez had any need to go back. In fact, the unit was moved from the thirteenth kilometre camp to -- to Bocija and Jablanica, I think the place was called, close to Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is that at no point in time leading immediately before the Farz operation, or during the operation, or shortly after did you visit the thirteenth kilometre camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say before the operation. Before the operation we would visit, because that is where the army was rallying. But afterwards. You asked me afterwards. Afterwards, I didn't go to the camp again at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We have heard during this trial that sometimes foreign combatants, enemy soldiers, would be decapitated. Did you ever hear or see any such decapitation or -- or combatants who had been decapitated?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may say that the last question by Judge Harhoff was perhaps misunderstood by the interpreter and it wasn't correctly interpreted. I think it's only fair to say that. The question that we heard in the Bosnian interpretation, the question by Judge Harhoff, was whether foreign fighters had their heads cut off, and I don't think that is quite the question put by the Judge as I was listening to English. For the sake of correctness towards the Trial Chamber and the witness that His Honour Judge Harhoff, if he considers it to be important, to repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't consider the question to be important given that I understood that the witness had never seen any signs of such decapitation. In that case my question becomes irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Mr. Awad, in your answer to some of the questions that were put to you by Judge Lattanzi, I -- I got a little confused, and I would like to get some clarification. You said that when you were given this uniform as a gift, the officer who gave it to you did not know of your intentions at the time to join the Mujahedin. Did I hear you correctly to say so to Judge Lattanzi?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what then would be the reason for him to give you, as a civilian, a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked for a uniform, and he gave it to me's knew me from before, and he probably hoped that through me he might receive some aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is new, that you asked for it. Anyway, that's okay. Now, I'm a little -- still a little puzzled that here is an officers in an army who can find it so easy to give government property to civilians. Is that normal?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: My dear Judge, people behaved as they wished, each on his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And they will behave according to laws also, don't they?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should behave according to laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And there are those who do keep to the laws. I want to find out what is wrong with this officer that makes him get -- step outside the law and give a civilian government property. What was wrong with him?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assumption is that he is not a professional soldier. He used to be a civilian, and in the war he became a soldier and a person who may not be familiar with the military rules. He behaved in the way he thought he could. I believe had he been a professional soldier, he certainly wouldn't have acted in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that answer. You also told us that there were two reasons for the Mujahedin that you belonged to to ask to be established and be -- be incorporated into the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The one reason was that you wanted to protect the local members of that Mujahedin from being accused of desertion. The other reason was that you wanted your Mujahedin to operate legally within the structure of the army. Is that correct? Did I summarise you correctly? All right.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. And if I remember you well, on Friday when you testified on this point and through your testimony on Friday, you were telling us that once established, it was operating within the structure. It was -- it was obedient and taking instructions. In fact, at some stage when you were referred by Madam Vidovic - I think it was yesterday - to a passage from one of your statements where you had indicated then, and I'm not talking about today, I'm talking about yesterday, where you indicated you were not instructions in that written statement, you said that was before the formation of the El Mujahid Detachment. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was meant was the determination of priority, where we would attack and along what axes and so on. Before the El Mujahedin Detachment was formed, we did not receive any instructions or any orders. But after the establishment of the detachment, the priorities of the attack would be determined by either the Operative Group or the corps command. And I repeat, we would be invited to come to discuss the issue. They would tell us that it was very important to gain control of a particular part of territory. We would engage in reconnaissance and so on. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're running far ahead of me. Just let me ask the questions, and listen to the questions and answer the questions. I'm still on these reasons for joining the ABiH. You -- you wanted the detachment or your group as a detachment within the army to operate within the law. That's how I understood you. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I'm wrong, just say I'm wrong. You see, you're going to try and give me an explanation. Have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We say that we wanted this group to be designated as such so that things happening around it should not be attributed to it, so that the group should have its own name and where it is acting. For example, we're in Mehurici, something happens in Travnik, and then people will say, "These Mujahedin." No. The Mujahedin at Mehurici had their name, the El Mujahedin. As for those in Travnik, I don't know about them, nor am I interested in them. That is why we wanted to be legality, not to act fully been the law as you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the point I'm trying to say. If I understood you well, when you explained this you said there were many other Mujahedins there who were committing illegal things, and you didn't want yours to commit illegal things, isn't it? You didn't want your group to be accused of the illegal things that are committed by the others. Therefore, you wanted to be -- stay within the legal organisation.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, do I understand by that that if anyone of the El Mujahedin Detachment, once established, committed a law -- a crime that broke the law of this country would -- how would it handle that situation? And I'm asking you this because you were asked today about infractions, and you said the Shura would discipline for infractions. I'm not talking about infractions. I'm talking about crimes, given that you wanted to on operate within the law.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that there were no infractions or measures -- I don't remember that there were any infractions that I could say this could be done in this way or another way. I don't remember any such infraction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me remind you. You told us about an infraction of one of your members who was detained for 15 days and was warned that he would be expelled if he repeated that. So that is an infraction. I'm talking of a crime. Let us assume that one of -- one of the El Mujahedin Detachment people killed somebody, killed a civilian. Not in combat, just in the street. Would that be for the Shura to deal with, or would that be for the laws of the country to deal with?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this didn't happen, and thank God it didn't, I cannot be specific what would happen. In 1993 an incident occurred when a humanitarian worker was killed, and two members of the El Mujahedin Detachment were arrested and put in gaol, but these men had nothing to do with that event. They were in a vehicle driven by the person who had carried out that attack and who was not a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment. They spent a month in prison. So if something like that happened, I believe that the people would be -- would have been arrested and put in gaol, as happened to these two men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the short answer is that, in fact, they would have been dealt with by the laws of the country, in terms of the laws of the country. That's your short answer. So that the Shura maintained discipline within the EMD, but crimes were always the responsibility of the state.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been like that, but thank God nothing like that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that you say nothing like that happened, but I just want to understand that -- what did you mean by wanting to operate within the law? Your second reason for wanting the join the army. You wanted to make sure that you stay within the laws of the country, and therefore you stay within the legal -- I'm trying to understand that, and I'm -- I'm saying if somebody within the EMD broke the law, would then the Shura take the law unto itself and -- and deal with that person, or would it hand him over to the law of the country to deal with him? Because if it would deal with him personally and not hand him over, then that second reason is not valid. So I'm trying to get a reconciliation between these two positions. What -- you wanted to operate within the law. What would you do if an EMD person committed a crime? When I say "you," I mean the EMD.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the Shura did nothing regarding those two men while they were in gaol. So it didn't interfere into that case. I believe it would have acted similarly had something like that, God forbid, happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You would have let the laws of the country take their course. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- very much. You told us that you saw two prisoners of war during this time. The other time you only heard about them. You didn't see them. Were you ever aware of any other people who were detained, whether they were prisoners of war or civilians?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detachment never had contacts with civilians. The detachment operations were exclusively conducted on military terrains: Hills, trenches, hand-to-hand fighting. I don't remember there being any other prisoners. For these others I knew, because I knew they were exchanged. I saw a list. I didn't hear of any others. I didn't hear of anyone else being captured, imprisoned, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Your statement has not been tendered into evidence, so I can't ask you my next question.

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not up to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. No, it has nothing to do with you. It's got to do with the lawyers. Don't you worry. Okay. I guess then that brings me to the end of my questions, because I can't take the matter any further. Any questions, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No questions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, just a few short questions. Further cross-examination by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Awad, I wanted to clarify this last topic that the Presiding Judge, His Honour Judge Moloto, asked you. As far as I understood your statement, and please correct me if I'm wrong, when you said that you decided to establish the detachment and to join the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you said that, "We wanted to become legal." Does that mean that you wished to be a unit of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? I hope that the Judges heard your answer. You said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you is this: At no point did you say that you had decided to accept all the laws of this country at that time?

utterances.speaker: AIMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say anything like that before. And the Judge insisted on specific things; could we act like this or like this. I believe it was possible to act like this. These are my views.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
